summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to change a model's behavior, style, or output format consistently, or when you want to compress domain knowledge and task patterns directly into model weights to reduce latency and per-token cost at scale. Prompt engineering is the right first step for most tasks and RAG is best when the model needs access to large, frequently-changing, or proprietary factual knowledge. Reach for fine-tuning only after prompting and RAG plateau, or when you need smaller/cheaper models to match larger ones on a narrow task.
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you need a consistent output style, tone, or structured format that prompting cannot reliably enforce across every request.
Choose fine-tuning when you have a stable, narrow task with enough high-quality labeled examples (typically hundreds to thousands) and want to reduce prompt length, latency, and cost.
Prefer RAG over fine-tuning when the knowledge is factual, large, or changes frequently, since RAG keeps data fresh without retraining.
Prefer prompt engineering first for prototyping, low-volume use, or when requirements are still evolving, reserving fine-tuning for proven high-volume production tasks.
